d.caption: Five pieces, and every algorithm in this course is a different choice of the first two. The last one is the piece people forget is separate: the loss is what the optimiser minimises, and the performance measure is what the business reads — and they are usually not the same function.

d.title: When to learn the rule, and when to write it
d.caption: Machine learning is the answer when the rule cannot be articulated, changes under you, varies per context, or is needed a million times. It is the wrong answer when the logic is known and deterministic — nobody should learn a tax bracket from data.

columns.title: Learn it
items: The rule cannot be articulated: which pixels make a cat
The rule changes: fraud adapts to whatever you block
The rule varies per context: what to recommend, now
The scale defeats manual rules: a billion events

columns.title: Write it
items: The logic is deterministic and known: tax brackets
There is no data, or far too little
The decision must be auditable line by line
A wrong answer is catastrophic and irreversible

d.caption: The signal decides the whole shape of the problem. Self-supervised is the one worth looking at twice: the label is manufactured from the input itself — the masked word, the next token — which is how a model trains on text nobody annotated.

d.title: What the table says before a model is fitted
d.caption: Each of these is cheap and each can end the project early — a target rate of 0.3% changes the metric, the threshold and the whole evaluation plan, and finding it on day one is worth more than any model. The leakage suspects found here are the ones 1.6 tests.

d.title: How many times each set may be read
d.caption: The validation set can be used repeatedly because nothing is reported from it — it only chooses. The test set is a one-shot measurement, and every look before the end spends some of its honesty, because you start making choices that fit it.

d.title: The scale case: what listwise deletion does to a million rows
d.caption: Two hundred columns, sixty of them missing 15% independently. The chance a row is complete is 0.85 to the power of 60, which is about one in seventeen thousand — so the 'safe' fix of dropping incomplete rows keeps **58** of the million. The naive fix destroys the dataset, and it does it silently.

nodes.label: Listwise deletion
nodes.sub: drop any row with a gap

d.title: The decomposition, in four moves
d.caption: Two cross terms vanish, and that is the whole derivation. The first because the noise is independent of the training set and has mean zero; the second because the average prediction minus its own average is zero by definition.

items.label: Substitute y = f + ε
items.desc: the world's output, split into signal and noise

items.label: Expand; the cross term is zero
items.desc: ε is independent of D and E[ε] = 0

items.label: Add and subtract the average prediction
items.desc: f-bar = the mean fit across training sets

items.label: Expand again; that cross term is zero too
bias-squared + variance + sigma-squared
items.desc: the third term is irreducible: no model beats it

d.title: Two thousand fits per degree, and the sum checks out
d.caption: Each row is two thousand polynomials of that degree, fitted to fresh samples of sin(πx) with σ = 0.3. Read down the columns: bias² collapses at degree 3 — a cubic can bend like one arch of a sine — and variance rises at every degree after. The **sum** column matches the measured test MSE to three decimals in every row, which is the derivation verified rather than assumed. And training MSE falls the whole way, passing below σ² = 0.09 from degree 3 on: the model is fitting noise, and the training error cannot tell you.

d.title: From a symptom to the dial that fixes it
d.caption: Two measurements separate every case: the training score, and the gap to validation. Reading them in this order means you never turn the wrong dial — and the commonest wasted month is spent collecting data for a bias problem, where more rows do nothing.

d.title: Three conditions that look alike on one number
d.caption: The training score alone cannot separate overfitting from leakage — both are high. What separates them is the validation score and what more data does: an overfit narrows with more rows, a leak does not narrow at all, because the leaking feature is just as informative in every fold.

d.title: L2 shrinks every weight; L1 sets some to exactly zero
d.caption: The difference is the shape of the penalty at the origin. L2's gradient vanishes as a weight approaches zero, so it never quite arrives; L1's gradient is a constant ±λ that does not weaken, so it pushes a weight all the way to zero and holds it there.

columns.title: L1 / lasso
items: Sets weights to exactly zero: selection
Picks one of a correlated group, arbitrarily

d.title: A penalty is a prior, and the penalised loss is a negative log posterior
d.caption: Take the log of prior × likelihood and the penalty falls out: a Gaussian prior's log is −w² (ridge), a Laplace prior's is −|w| (lasso). So MAP estimation **is** penalised fitting, and λ is the prior's confidence — which is why a stronger penalty is the same statement as a tighter belief that the weights are small.

columns.title: Gaussian prior → L2
items: λ is the inverse prior variance

columns.title: Laplace prior → L1
items: Mass concentrated at zero plus heavy tails
Believes most weights are truly zero

d.title: Early stopping: the round where validation turns
d.caption: Six hundred boosting rounds on the same data. Training loss falls monotonically the whole way — it always will — while validation bottoms out at round 45 and then climbs. By round 600 the training loss is a **sixth** of its value at the minimum and the validation loss is 62% worse. The curve is the regulariser: stop where the second column turns.

d.title: One split is a lottery; the same data, the same model
d.caption: Twenty 70/30 splits of one dataset, one model, nothing else changed. The worst split reports 0.695 and the best 0.813 — a spread wide enough to 'prove' almost any comparison you like. Cross-validation does not make the model better; it makes the **estimate** stable, and the sd falls from 0.028 to 0.004 as the folds increase.

d.title: The fold must match the deployment
d.caption: A fold strategy is a claim about what the model will meet. Get it wrong in the direction of ease and the score is not pessimistic or noisy — it is wrong: 0.995 for a model that had memorised entity ids.

d.title: Nested cross-validation: one loop chooses, the other measures
d.caption: The inner loop picks the hyperparameters on the training part of each outer fold; the outer loop scores the **whole procedure**, including the picking, on rows it never saw. One loop cannot do both jobs, because the score that chose the winner is the maximum of many noisy numbers and is therefore optimistic by construction.

d.title: Four kinds of leakage, each with the score it produced here
d.caption: Every pair is the same data and the same model, differing only in whether the leak is present. The second row is the one to remember: a **200-level column of pure noise** scored 0.836 when target-encoded on all rows, and 0.468 — chance — when the encoder was fitted inside the fold.

d.title: Where the fit happens decides whether the score is real
d.caption: The two paths differ by **one line's position**. Fit the encoder above the split and it has seen every row's label, so a 200-level noise column carries the target into the model and scores 0.836. Move the same encoder inside the fold and it scores 0.468 — chance, which is the truth about a noise column.

d.title: A centred window reads the future; a trailing one does not
d.caption: A 7-day rolling mean **centred** on day t averages days t−3 to t+3 — so the feature for Wednesday contains Saturday. It scored 0.771 against 0.618 for the trailing version and 0.571 for the raw value, and that 0.15 of apparent skill is entirely the three days that had not happened yet.

d.title: What each transform leaks when it is fitted before the split
d.caption: The severity is set by what the transform saw. A scaler learns a mean; a target encoder learns the **label**, at group resolution, which is why it can turn a noise column into a 0.836. All of them have the same fix, and it is one line: make the transform a step in the Pipeline.

d.title: Why restricting the hypothesis space is the whole trick
d.caption: Empirical risk minimisation picks the candidate with the lowest training error. With an unrestricted space that is always a lookup table — zero training error, no generalisation. The bound says the gap between training and true error grows with the space's capacity and shrinks with n, so the only way to learn is to **search a space small enough that fitting it means something**.

nodes.label: ERM
nodes.sub: pick the lowest training error in H

d.title: Every family is an assumption about the world
d.caption: There is no assumption-free learner — that is the no-free-lunch theorem stated usefully. Choosing a model is choosing which bias you believe, so the column that matters is the last one: what the family cannot see however much data you give it.
cells: the target is a weighted sum

d.title: Three axes that place any model
d.caption: These are independent choices, and each one predicts a specific behaviour. The third explains a cost that only appears in production: a lazy model has no training time and pays at every query instead — 382 ms per 5,000 rows against 0.5 ms for an eager one.

cells.text: eager: at fit time, 0.5 ms to score

d.title: The curse of dimensionality, measured
d.caption: Five hundred uniform points in the unit cube, and one query point. Read the ratio column: the nearest neighbour goes from 0.2% of the farthest distance at d = 1 to **86%** at d = 500, so distance stops discriminating and every method whose whole idea is 'nearby points are similar' loses its meaning. The last column is the same fact from the other side — by 100 dimensions every point is on the surface.

d.title: Gradient descent on five points, and the step size that breaks it
d.caption: The Hessian here is constant with eigenvalues 0.338 and 23.66, so the stability limit is 2/23.66 = **0.0845**. At η = 0.02 the loss falls to 0.024 — but after two hundred steps b is still 0.17 against a true 0.05, because it crawls along the flat direction whose eigenvalue is 0.34. At η = 0.10, just above the limit, every step overshoots further than the last and the loss reaches 22,640 by iteration 10. The closed form is w = 1.99, b = 0.05.

d.title: Batch, mini-batch, stochastic
d.caption: The gradient gets noisier and the updates get more frequent as you move right, and mini-batch wins because both of those are useful: enough updates to make progress, enough rows to vectorise, and enough noise to leave a bad basin.

d.title: Reading a loss curve
d.caption: Five of these six are optimisation problems with an optimisation fix. The last one is not — a training loss that is fine while validation rises is overfitting, and no change to the learning rate will touch it.

d.title: Five residuals, four losses, and what the outlier does to each
d.caption: The same five residuals throughout; the 8.0 is the outlier. Squared error charges it **32.0** of the 34.7 total, so the fit chases it — and its gradient pulls sixteen times harder than the 0.5's. Absolute error charges 8.0 and pulls on every row with identical force. Huber is squared inside |r| ≤ 1 and linear outside, which caps the outlier's gradient at 1.0. The last row is the point: squared error's optimum is the mean, absolute error's is the median, and the quantile loss's is the quantile.
